title: Physical predetermination to intrinsically evil acts seems to make God the author of sin
source_text: LVI. In primis autem percipere non possum quomodo statui possit, Deum causas liberas, etiam ad actus intrinsece malos Physice praemovere, & praedeterminare, quin inde sequatur Deum esse peccati authorem. Quis enim capiat, exempli gratia, Deum influxu quodam omnem humanae voluntatis motum antecedente, imposuisse primo homini necessitatem fructum vetitum appetendi, & appetitum comedendi: atque etiam quotidie efficientia quadam proprie dicta, homines praedeterminare, & ut sic barbare loquar necessitare ad hoc ut Deum blasphement, & eum odio habeant; & tamen culpam, quae ab istis actibus separari non potest, in Deum ipsum refundendam non esse?
pass_a_gloss: But in the first place I cannot perceive how it can be laid down, that God physically premoves, and predetermines free causes even to acts intrinsically evil, without it following thence that God is the author of sin. For who could comprehend, for example, that God by some influence preceding every motion of the human will, imposed on the first man a necessity of desiring the forbidden fruit, and a desire of eating: and also daily by an efficiency properly so called, predetermines men, and that I may speak so barbarously necessitates them to this that they blaspheme God, and hold him in hatred; and yet that the blame, which cannot be separated from those acts, is not to be poured back upon God himself?
pass_b_english: Above all, I cannot see how anyone can hold that God physically premoves and predetermines free causes even to acts that are intrinsically evil without its following that God is the author of sin.

Who could understand, for instance, that God, by an influence preceding every motion of the human will, laid on the first man a necessity of desiring the forbidden fruit and an appetite for eating it; and that every day, by an efficient causality in the proper sense, he predetermines people, and, to use a barbarous word, 'necessitates' them to blaspheme God and hate him; and yet that the guilt, which cannot be separated from those acts, is not to be laid back on God himself?

lemmas.gloss: that I may speak so barbarously, necessitate

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
